Spontaneous Abortion

  • Loss of a clinically recognized pregnancy before 20 weeks’ gestation or <500 g.
  • Make up 15 – 20% of clinically diagnosed pregnancies.
  • Risk factors include advanced maternal age, increasing gravidity, prior miscarriage and smoking.
  • History: Vaginal bleeding is the most common presenting complaint, followed by crampy abdominal pain.
  • Examination: Initially, vital signs should be taken to rule out hemodynamic instability. Speculum examination allows visualization of the cervix and potentially the location of products of conception. Bimanual examination may help estimate gestational age.
  • Laboratory tests: Serum human choronic gonadotropin (hCG), blood count and rhesus (Rh) typing should be sent (virtually all Rh-negative patients should receive anti-D immunoglobulin prophylaxis.

Causes:

  • More than 80% of all miscarriages occur in the first trimester (<12 weeks’ gestation). The exact mechanisms are not always apparent, but death of the embryo or fetus nearly always precedes spontaneous expulsion. As a result, finding the cause of early miscarriage involves ascertaining the cause of fetal death. At least half result from chromosomal abnormalities.
  • Less than 20% of all miscarriages occur in the second trimester (12 – 20 weeks’ gestation). The fetus frequently does not die before expulsion and anatomic factors are more likely to be causative.

Incomplete miscarriage

  • Incomplete miscarriages usually occur between 6 and 14 weeks gestation.
  • Here the entire products of conception are not expelled but a part is left inside the uterine cavity.
  • Sign and Symptoms:
  • Uterine bleeding with cervical dilation but with incomplete expulsion of the product of conception (POC).
  • Continuous, colicky lower abdominal pain
  • Size of uterus: Smaller
  • Internal Os: Open
  • Investigation: Retained products in USG
  • Management:
  • If the patient is in shock due to blood loss, she should be resuscitated before any active treatment is undertaken.
  • In case of early abortion (before 12 weeks’), dilation and evacuation under general anesthesia is to be done.
  • In late abortion, uterus is evacuated under general anesthesia and the products are removed by ovum forceps or by blunt curette. The remove products are subjected to a histological examination.

Complete miscarriage

  • Complete miscarriages are most common <6 or >14 weeks’.
  • Here the products of conception are expelled in masse.
  • Sign and Symptoms: Uterine bleeding with complete expulsion of the product of conception (POC) and closed cervical os.
  • Size of uterus: Smaller
  • Internal Os: Closed
  • Investigation:
  • On examination, the expelled flashy mass is found.
  • USG: Cavity empty
  • Management:
  • Complete miscarriages may be managed expectantly without evacuation.

Missed abortion

  • Fetal demise before 20 weeks’ gestation without detachment of the placenta – resulting in retention of products of conception for days or weeks behind a closed cervical os.
  • When the fetus is dead and retained inside the uterus for a variable period, it is known as missed abortion
  • Continuous brown vaginal discharge occurs after the demise.
  • Many women have no other symptoms.
  • Size of uterus: Smaller
  • Internal Os: Closed

    • Dead fetus
    • A nonviable pregnancy without vaginal bleeding, uterine cramping or cervical dilation.
    • Mean sac diameter ≥25 mm or crown rump length ≥ 7 mm with no fetal heart beat.
    • Coagulopathy also very rarely seen due to prolonged retention of a dead fetus after mid pregnancy.
  • Management:
    • It is individualized, depending on the circumstances.
    • Medical management is often the safest option. Conservative management awaiting a spontaneous completed abortion or induce contractions with misoprostol (Cytotec®) (PGE1).
    • Scheduled suction D&C, conservative management awaiting a spontaneous completed abortion or induce contractions with misoprostol (Cytotec) (PGE1).
    • Expectant management is often difficult for the patient to endure after being informed of the demise.

• Bedsores can happen when a person is bedridden or otherwise immobile, unconscious or unable to sense pain.

  • Pressure score occurs if external pressure exceeds 30 mmHg of capillary occlusive pressure.
  • Tissue necrosis with prolonged pressure.
  • It is also known as bed sores, pressure ulcers, decubitus ulcers.
  • Incidence: 5% in hospitalized patient.
  • Pressure sore is most common in: Ischium > Greater trochanter > Sacrum in the gluteal region.

Table: Classification of Pressure Sores

Stage

  Management

1

Non-blanchable erythema without a breach in the epidermis

  • If the cause is direct pressure then either ensure that the patient’s position is changed more frequently or ‘step-up’ the pressure relief, e.g. move the patient from a static foam mattress to an alternating pressure mattress.
  • The skin in a grade 1 pressure ulcer is not broken but it requires protection and monitoring.
  • Wound dressings for a grade 1 pressure ulcer should be simple (Dressing should not be done for stage 1 as skin is intact) and offer protection without risking any further skin damage, especially if the patient is sliding down the bed or chair causing the dressing to ‘ruck’.
  • A film dressing or a thin hydrocolloid would be appropriate to protect the wound area.
  • The slippery nature of these dressings may reduce further friction or shearing if these factors are involved.

2

Partial-thickness skin loss involving the epidermis and dermis

  • If the pressure ulcer is circular, this is often an indication that direct pressure is the cause. In this case ensure that the patient’s position is changed more frequently or ‘step-up’ the level of pressure relief.
  • If the pressure ulcer is not uniform and is more widespread, then shearing or friction may be the cause.
  • A grade 2 pressure ulcer is a superficial wound. If the wound has slough on the wound bed, debridement may be necessary.
  • There are many dressings that aid debridement, for example, hydrogels or hydrocolloids.
  • If protection is necessary as well as the promotion of a moist wound healing environment, a hydrocolloid or foam may be appropriate.
  • Dressing some areas may be a challenge like in sacral and heel region. So sacral flap also used.

3

Full-thickness skin loss extending into the subcutaneous tissue but not through underlying fascia

  • The damaging factors (pressure, shear or friction) are continuing.
  • The dressings are not managing the exudate levels and the wound is getting bigger or deeper due to the destructive nature of chronic exudate
  • The pressure ulcer may be infected
  • The patient has a poor ability to heal, which may be due to poor circulation, inadequate nutrition, low hemoglobin levels or the presence of disease such as diabetes mellitus.
  •  As these pressure ulcers are substantially deep in many cases, the absorbency levels of the dressings may need to be increased.
  • Alginates and Foams absorbent dressings can be used in combination to increase the overall absorbency.
  • If this is occurring after the absorbent dressings, increase the dressing absorbency levels or the frequency of dressing changes.
  • If conventional dressings cannot manage the exudate, topical negative pressure therapy could be considered.

4

Full-thickness skin loss through fascia with extensive tissue destruction, may be involving muscles, one, tendon or joint.

  • Grade 4 pressure ulcers are the deepest. It is essential to establish if or why the wound is deteriorating or if the depth of the wound is due to the initial pressure damage.
  • The steps outlined under the treatment of grade 3 pressure ulcers should be followed.
  • If there is bone exposed, consider infection in the bone (osteomyelitis). This can be identified using an X-ray or a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans and is usually treatable with antibiotic therapy.

• Temporal pulse - The temporal pulse (i.e. superficial temporal artery) is palpated on the temple directly in front of the ear with the index finger.
  • Carotid artery pulse - The common carotid artery is palpated on the neck below the jaw and lateral to the larynx/trachea (i.e. mid-point between your earlobe and chin) using the middle and index fingers.
  • Brachial artery pulse - The brachial artery is palpated on the anterior aspect of the elbow by gently pressing the artery against the underlying bone with the middle and index fingers. The brachial artery pulse is commonly used to measure blood pressure with a stethoscope and sphygmomanometer.
  • Radial artery pulse - The radial pulse is palpated immediately above the wrist joint near the base of the thumb (i.e. common site) or in the anatomical snuff box (i.e. alternative site), by gently pressing the radial artery against the underlying bone with the middle and index fingers.

  • Posterior tibial pulse - The posterior tibial pulse is palpated posterior and inferior to the medial malleolus by gently pressing the tibial artery against the underlying bone with the middle and index fingers.
  • Dorsalis pedis pulse - The dorsalis pedis pulse is palpated in the groove between the first and second toes slightly medial on the dorsum of the foot (i.e. dorsal-lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon and distal to the dorsal prominence of the navicular bone) with the middle and/or index fingers.
  • Apical pulse - The unilateral apical pulse (i.e. apex of the heart) can be located in the fifth intercostal space immediately to the left of the sternum using a stethoscope. Presentation: This refers to the part of the fetus that is closest to the cervix and pelvic inlet during labor. The most common types of presentation are:

  • Cephalic: The head is the presenting part (most common).
  • Breech: The buttocks or feet are presenting.

  • Lie: This describes the relationship of the long axis of the fetus to the long axis of the mother. The two main types of lie are:
  • Longitudinal: The fetus is oriented vertically (head or buttocks up).
  • Transverse: The fetus is oriented horizontally.
  • Denominator: This term usually refers to a specific landmark on the presenting part of the fetus that helps in determining its position. For example, in a cephalic presentation, the occiput (the back of the head) is often used as the denominator.
  • Position: This describes the specific orientation of the presenting part relative to the mother's pelvis. It is usually expressed in terms of the fetal back's position (anterior, posterior, or lateral) in relation to the mother's pelvis.

  • Cleft lip repair, usually performed by a plastic surgeon, is a major part of the treatment of a newborn with cleft lip, palate or both; some surgeons favor early repair, before the newborn is discharged from the hospital; other surgeons prefer to wait until the newborn is 1 to 2 months old, weighs about 10 lbs and is gaining weight steadily.
  • Child who has had a cleft lip repair should be positioned on their side or back to keep them from rubbing their face in the bed.
  • A child with only a cleft palate repair may sleep on their stomach. It is important to keep the stitches clean and without crusting.
  • Nursing interventions for the patient with cleft lip and palate are:
    • Maintain adequate nutrition: Breastfeeding may be successful because the breast tissue may mold to close the gap; if the newborn cannot be breastfed, the mother’s breast milk may be expressed and used instead of formula; a soft nipple with a cross-cut made to promote easy flow of milk may work well.
    • Positioning: If the cleft lip is unilateral, the nipple should be aimed at the unaffected side; the infant should be kept in an upright position during feeding.
    • Tools for feeding: Lamb’s nipples (extra-long nipples) and special cleft palate nipples molded to fit into the open palate area to close the gap may be used; one of the simplest and most effective methods may be the use of an eyedropper or an Asepto syringe with a short piece of rubber tubing on the tip (Breck feeder).
    • Promote family coping: Encourage the family to verbalize their feelings regarding the defect and their disappointment; serve as a model for the family caregiver’s attitudes toward the child.
    • Reduce family anxiety: Give the family information about cleft repairs; encourage them to ask questions and reassure them that any question is valid.
    • Provide family teaching: Explain the usual routine of preoperative, intraoperative and post-operative care; written information is helpful, but be certain the parents understand the information.

choices.correct_explanation:
STAGES OF PRESSURE ULCER

  • Bedsores can happen when a person is bedridden or otherwise immobile, unconscious or unable to sense pain.
  • Bedsores are ulcers that happen on areas of the skin that are under pressure from lying in bed, sitting in a wheelchair or wearing a cast for a prolonged time.
  • Pressure score occurs if external pressure exceeds 30 mmHg of capillary occlusive pressure.
  • Tissue necrosis with prolonged pressure.
  • It is also known as Bed sores, pressure ulcers, Decubitus ulcers.
  • Incidence: 5% in hospitalized patient.
  • Pressure sores are most common in: Ischium > Greater trochanter > Sacrum in the gluteal region.
  • After Gluteal region the site in order are: Heel > Lateral malleoli > occipital region.

          Table: Classification of Pressure Sores

Stage

 Description

   Cause

  Management

1

Non-blanchable erythema without a breach in the epidermis
  • If the cause is direct pressure then either ensure that the patient’s position is changed more frequently or ‘step-up’ the pressure relief, e.g. move the patient from a static foam mattress to an alternating pressure mattress.
  •  The skin in a grade 1 pressure ulcer is not broken but it requires protection and monitoring.
  •  Wound dressings for a grade 1 pressure ulcer should be simple and offer protection without risking any further skin damage, especially if the patient is sliding down the bed or chair causing the dressing to ‘ruck’.
  •     A film dressing or a thin hydrocolloid would be appropriate to protect the wound area.
  •     The slippery nature of these dressings may reduce further friction or shearing if these factors are involved.

2

Partial-thickness skin loss involving the epidermis and dermis
  • If the pressure ulcer is circular, this is often an indication that direct pressure is the cause. In this case ensure that the patient’s position is changed more frequently or ‘step-up’ the level of pressure relief.
  • If the pressure ulcer is not uniform and is more widespread, then shearing or friction may be the cause.
  • A grade 2 pressure ulcer is a superficial wound. If the wound has slough on the wound bed, debridement may be necessary.
  • There are many dressings that aid debridement, for example, hydrogels or hydrocolloids.
  • If protection is necessary as well as the promotion of a moist wound healing environment, a hydrocolloid or foam may be appropriate.
  • Dressing some areas may be a challenge like in sacral and heel region. So sacral flap is  used.

3

Full-thickness skin loss extending into the subcutaneous tissue but not through underlying fascia
  • The damaging factors (pressure, shear or friction) are continuing.
  • The dressings are not managing the exudate levels and the wound is getting bigger or deeper due to the destructive nature of chronic exudate
  • The pressure ulcer may be infected
  • The patient has a poor ability to heal, which may be due to poor circulation, inadequate nutrition, low hemoglobin levels or the presence of disease such as diabetes mellitus.
  • As these pressure ulcers are substantially deep in many cases, the absorbency levels of the dressings may need to be increased.
  • Alginates and Foams absorbent dressings can be used in combination to increase the overall absorbency.
  • If this is occurring after the absorbent dressings, increase the dressing absorbency levels or the frequency of dressing changes.
  • If conventional dressings cannot manage the exudate, topical negative pressure therapy could be considered.

4

Full-thickness skin loss through fascia with extensive tissue destruction, may be involving muscles, one, tendon or joint.
  • Grade 4 pressure ulcers are the deepest. It is essential to establish if or why the wound is deteriorating or if the depth of the wound is due to the initial pressure damage.
  • The steps outlined under the treatment of grade 3 pressure ulcers should be followed.
  • If there is bone exposed, consider infection in the bone (osteomyelitis). This can be identified using an X-ray or a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans and is usually treatable with antibiotic therapy.


Figure 1: Stages of Pressure Ulcer

  • Prevention is the best treatment:
    • Bedridden patients be turned every 2 hours
    • Wheel chair patient should lift themselves every 10 minutes for 10 seconds.
    • Provide air mattress bedding.
  • Treatment:
    • Debridement
    • VAC devices at negative -125 mmHg suction pressure.
    • Flaps

        Figure 2: Sacral dressing

Clinical Pearls:

  • During dressing for pressure ulcers: Keep the ulcer tissue moist and surrounding skin dry.

choices.correct_explanation:
• Fetal Lie: Using the techniques described above, the clinician should be able to develop an assessment of the relationship between the fetal and maternal dorsal columns (the longitudinal axis of the human body). If the fetus and maternal column are parallel (on the same long axis), the lie is termed as vertical or longitudinal lie. This is the most common lie of fetuses in labor.
  • Attitude: In addition to lie, the fetus has an attitude. This is defined as the relationship between various parts of the fetus to each other. In the normal attitude, the fetus is in universal flexion. It enables the fetus to occupy the least amount of space in the intrauterine cavity. The fetal attitude is extremely difficult, if not impossible, to assess without the help of an ultrasound examination.
  • Presentation: After the lie of the fetus is assessed, the clinician has to detail the fetus further by describing the lowermost structure of the fetus in the maternal pelvis. This is referred to as the fetal presentation. In the vertical (or longitudinal) lie, the fetal presentation can be either cephalic or breech. In the transverse lie, the presentation is usually the back or shoulder & in the oblique lie, it is usually the shoulder or the arm.
  • Position: The next step in the assessment of the fetus consists of determining the position of the presenting part. This is a description of the relation between the presenting part of the fetus and the maternal pelvis. In the case of a longitudinal lie with a vertex presentation, the occiput of the fetal calvarium is the landmark used to describe the position. When the occiput is facing the maternal pubic symphysis, the position is termed as direct occiput anterior. If the occiput is between the ischial spines and the symphysis, it is called either a right or left occiput anterior. If the occiput is located halfway between the promontories of the sacrum and the symphysis, the position is termed as either a left or right occiput transverse. As the occiput approaches the sacrum, it becomes either a right or left occiput posterior. When the occiput is straight down (i.e., facing the sacrum or coccyx), the position is called direct occiput posterior.

Reference:

  1. Kaur S.2023.Textbook of Midwifery and Obstetrical for BSC Nursing Student.2nd ed.CBS Publishers.p.75

• The fallopian tubes are bilateral conduits between the ovaries and the uterus in the female pelvis. They function as channels for oocyte transport and fertilization. Given this role, the fallopian tubes are a common etiology of infertility as well as the target of purposeful surgical sterilization.
  • The implantation normally takes place in the superior and posterior walls of the uterine body (corpus uteri) in the functional layer of the endometrium during the secretory phase of the cycle. Normal implantation zone of the blastocyst in the superior and posterior wall of the uterine cavity.
  • Sperm production takes place inside the seminiferous tubules, which is a convoluted cluster of tubes located inside the testes. Testosterone production occurs in cells surrounding the seminiferous tubules, called Leydig cells.
  • The ovaries produce the egg cells, called the ova or oocytes. The oocytes are then transported to the fallopian tube where fertilization by a sperm may occur. The fertilized egg then moves to the uterus, where the uterine lining has thickened in response to the normal hormones of the reproductive cycle.

choices.correct_explanation:
BCG (TB) vaccine side effects

  • Reactions to the BCG vaccine are uncommon and generally mild.
  • The most common side effects include fever, headache and swollen glands.
  • More serious complications, such as abscesses or bone inflammation, are rare.
  • Most children develop a sore at the injection site. Once healed, the sore may leave a small scar. This is normal and nothing to worry about.

BCG vaccination scar

  • Virtually everyone when given the BCG vaccination will develop a raised bubble at the site of the injection, which may disappear soon afterwards.
  • About 2 to 6 weeks after the injection, a small spot may appear at the site of the injection.
  • It's normal for the spot to turn into a blister, which sometimes oozes before becoming a crusty scab.
  • It's important to leave the area uncovered as the air will help it to heal. It's normal for it to leave a small scar.
  • Occasionally, there may be a more severe skin reaction, but this should heal within several weeks.

Reference:

  1. Ghai O.P.2023.Ghai Essential Pediatrics. 10th ed. CBS Publishers.p.187 - 189.
